facts.fact_text: On 30 October 1998, the applicant notified the Salzburg Federal Police Authority (Bundespolizeidirektion) under section 2 of the Assembly Act (Versammlungsgesetz) of a planned meeting.

The applicant notified the Salzburg Federal Police Authority that on All Saints' Day, 1 November 1998, from 9 a.m. until 1 p.m., he would be holding a meeting at the Salzburg municipal cemetery in front of the war memorial.
The purpose of the applicant's planned meeting was to commemorate the Salzburg Jews killed by the SS during the Second World War.
The applicant expected about six participants at the planned meeting.
The participants of the applicant's planned meeting would carry commemorative messages in their hands and attached to their clothes.
The applicant stated that no other means of expression, such as chanting or banners, which might offend piety or undermine public order would be used at the planned meeting.
On 31 October 1998, the Salzburg Federal Police Authority prohibited the applicant's planned meeting.
The Salzburg Federal Police Authority ordered that any remedies used against its decision to prohibit the applicant's planned meeting should not have suspensive effect.
As a result of the Salzburg Federal Police Authority's order that remedies should not have suspensive effect, the applicant's planned demonstration could not take place.
The Salzburg Federal Police Authority relied on section 6 of the Assembly Act (Versammlungsgesetz) when prohibiting the applicant's planned meeting.
The Assembly Act 1953 (Versammlungsgesetz) regulates the exercise of the right to freedom of assembly in Austria.

Section 2(1) of the Assembly Act 1953 (Versammlungsgesetz) provides that any person intending to organise a public assembly or any assembly which is generally open to persons other than invited guests must give the authorities notice in writing at least twenty-four hours in advance.
Section 2(1) of the Assembly Act 1953 (Versammlungsgesetz) requires that the written notice indicate the purpose, place and time of the meeting.
Pursuant to section 6 of the Assembly Act 1953 (Versammlungsgesetz), the competent authority must prohibit any assembly which would contravene criminal law or endanger public order and security.
The Salzburg Federal Police Authority prohibited the applicant's planned meeting on the ground that it would endanger public order and security.

The Salzburg Federal Police Authority found that disruption of the Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) commemoration ceremony and other commemoration ceremonies was likely to offend the religious feelings of members of the public visiting the cemetery.

The Salzburg Federal Police Authority found that disruption of the commemoration ceremonies would indisputably be regarded as disrespectful towards the dead soldiers of both world wars and thus as an unbearable provocation.

The Salzburg Federal Police Authority found that there was a risk of protests by visitors to the cemetery which could degenerate into open conflict between them and those participating in the applicant's planned assembly.
The Salzburg Public Security Authority (Sicherheitsdirektion) concluded that the prohibition of the applicant's planned assembly was necessary for the maintenance of public order.

The Salzburg Public Security Authority (Sicherheitsdirektion) concluded that the prohibition of the applicant's planned assembly was necessary for the protection of the Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) commemoration ceremony.

The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) found that the authorities had correctly assumed that the prohibition of the assembly planned by the applicant was necessary to protect the general public against potential disturbances.

The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) found that the prohibition of the applicant's assembly was necessary under Article 11 § 2 of the Convention for the protection of the rights and freedoms of others.
The applicant noted that the planned meeting would coincide with the gathering of Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV).
The applicant considered the gathering of Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) to be unlawful.

The assembly of Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) was to be held at the same time and place as the applicant's planned meeting, namely on 1 November 1998 at the Salzburg municipal cemetery in front of the war memorial.
F.E. refused to give an undertaking that the proposed meeting in memory of the murdered Salzburg Jews would not disrupt the Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) gathering.
The Salzburg Federal Police Authority noted that Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) was a registered association.
Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV), like a number of other organisations, traditionally held a commemoration ceremony at the Salzburg municipal cemetery on All Saints' Day.

The Salzburg Federal Police Authority noted that such commemorations by Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) qualified as popular ceremonies within the meaning of section 5 of the Assembly Act (Versammlungsgesetz) and thus did not require authorisation.

The Salzburg Federal Police Authority found that disruption of the Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) commemoration ceremony and other commemoration ceremonies was likely to offend the religious feelings of members of the public visiting the cemetery.

The Salzburg Federal Police Authority found that disruption of the commemoration ceremonies would indisputably be regarded as disrespectful towards the dead soldiers of both world wars and thus as an unbearable provocation.

The Salzburg Federal Police Authority found that there was a risk of protests by visitors to the cemetery which could degenerate into open conflict between them and those participating in the applicant's planned assembly.
The Salzburg Public Security Authority (Sicherheitsdirektion) noted that Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) was a registered association whose members were mainly former members of the SS.

For more than forty years, members of Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) had commemorated SS soldiers killed in the Second World War by gathering on All Saints' Day and laying a wreath in front of the war memorial at the Salzburg municipal cemetery.
In the years prior to 1999, a number of organisations had organised protest campaigns with the aim of disrupting the Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) commemoration ceremony.

The protest campaigns against the Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) commemoration ceremony had led to vehement discussions with members of Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) and other visitors to the cemetery.
The protest campaigns against the Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) commemoration ceremony had required intervention by the police.

The Salzburg Public Security Authority (Sicherheitsdirektion), referring to the submissions of F.E., found that the assembly planned by the applicant was also aimed at a confrontation with Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV).
The Salzburg Public Security Authority (Sicherheitsdirektion) concluded that the prohibition of the applicant's planned assembly was necessary for the maintenance of public order.

The Salzburg Public Security Authority (Sicherheitsdirektion) concluded that the prohibition of the applicant's planned assembly was necessary for the protection of the Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) commemoration ceremony.

The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) observed that the authorities deciding on the prohibition of an assembly had to weigh the applicant's interest in holding the meeting against the public interests enumerated in Article 11 § 2 of the Convention.

The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) stated that the prohibition of the applicant's proposed meeting would not be justified if its sole purpose were to protect the Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) commemoration ceremony.

The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) expressed doubts as to the authorities' assessment that the Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) commemoration was a popular ceremony within the meaning of section 5 of the Assembly Act (Versammlungsgesetz) and therefore did not require authorisation.

The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) found that the prohibition of the applicant's planned meeting was justified for reasons other than the protection of the Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) commemoration ceremony.
The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) noted that the gathering of Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) had in previous years been the target of activities aimed at disrupting it.

The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) noted that the activities aimed at disrupting the Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) gathering had caused considerable nuisance to other visitors of the cemetery.
The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) noted that the activities aimed at disrupting the Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV) gathering had each time required police intervention.

The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) found that the authorities had correctly assumed that the prohibition of the assembly planned by the applicant was necessary to protect the general public against potential disturbances.

The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) observed that All Saints' Day is an important religious holiday on which the population traditionally visits cemeteries in order to commemorate the dead.
The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) observed that the commemoration of the dead as a religious tradition is protected by Article 9 of the Convention.

The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) observed that Article 9 of the Convention contains a positive obligation for the State to protect persons manifesting their religion against deliberate disturbance by others.
